newsitem.title: USA: S&P gives tepid review to state lotteries.
newsitem.headline: S&P gives tepid review to state lotteries.

text.p: Although states are becoming increasingly dependent on lottery revenues to meet budget goals, the practice can have several negative consequences on credit quality, Standard & Poor's Corp said Monday. In an analysis published in CreditWeek Municipal, S&P said lotteries have been used like one-shot revenue resources for long-term capital costs and help state officials "avoid difficult decisions that proper budgeting tools would require."

The use of lotteries to secure bond financings "increases overall debt burden without stimulating the economic growth and may thus negatively impact municipal ratings," S&P said. In a review of the lottery experiences of several states, S&P pointed in particular to problems in California. The agency said the state "bungled" a new lottery computer contract and was saddled with $44 million in unexpected expenses.
"The loss may have cost California schools up to $113 million in anticipated revenue," S&P said.

In Georgia, lottery revenues are expected to contribute $546 million to the budget. But increases in lottery revenues are offset by comparable decreases in state tax dollars, which are a more predictable source of revenue.
"South Carolina is a notable exception that has not jumped on the jackpot bandwagon," S&P said. The state Legislature failed to muster a two-thirds majority in January to approve a lottery.

Countrywide, lottery sales have increased 94.3 percent between fiscal years 1990 and 1996, according to S&P. As of April, five states have land-based casinos, six have riverboat gambling, and 18 have Indian casinos.
